# The rules a firm actually follows {background-color="#E3120B" style="color:#F7F4ED"}

## Count the rules in a phone

| Rule | Written by |
|---|---|
| The radio interface | 3GPP — an industry partnership |
| Wi-Fi | IEEE — a professional association |
| The charging port | a private consortium — then made mandatory by the EU |
| The factory's quality and environmental systems | ISO 9001, ISO 14001 |
| The supplier's minerals due diligence | OECD guidance, industry schemes, buyer codes |

::: {.get}
**Private authority:** non-state actors making rules others treat as binding. For a firm, a **risk** — and a **lever**.
:::

# The governance triangle {background-color="#E3120B" style="color:#F7F4ED"}

## Abbott & Snidal (2009)

```
                       STATE
                        /\
                       /  \
                      /    \
                     /      \
                    /________\
                FIRM          NGO
```

- Near a **corner**: one actor type — industry code, activist label, treaty
- In the **middle**: hybrids — multi-stakeholder certification; the UN Global Compact
- **The shadow of the state**: private schemes are shaped by the threat — or promise — of public regulation

::: {.muted}
In W. Mattli & N. Woods (Eds.), *The Politics of Global Regulation*, Princeton UP, pp. 44–88.
:::

## Put it to the room

> Place these in the triangle: **FSC**, **UN Global Compact**, **ISO 14001**, **an industry code of conduct**, **the EU's common charger rule**.

::: {.warn}
The placement predicts the behaviour: who can change the scheme, who finds it legitimate, whether a state may make it mandatory.
:::

# Standards and power {background-color="#E3120B" style="color:#F7F4ED"}

## Who wins at ISO and the IEC? Mattli & Büthe (2003)

| Explanation | Prediction |
|---|---|
| **Technological rationality** | the best technology wins |
| **Primacy of power** | the largest markets win |
| **Institutional complementarity** | those whose **domestic** standard-setting matches the international structure win |

::: {.fragment}
::: {.get}
Their evidence favours **institutional complementarity**: coordinated European national bodies were better placed than the fragmented US system.
:::
:::

::: {.muted}
*World Politics*, 56(1), 1–42. [doi:10.1353/wp.2004.0006](https://doi.org/10.1353/wp.2004.0006)
:::

## Technical standards are geopolitics

- **Telecoms** — whose patents and specifications are in the next generation?
- **Batteries and charging** — whose formats become the default?
- **AI and data** — whose rules does a global firm adopt everywhere?

::: {.step}
**The Brussels effect** (Bradford, 2020): it is often cheaper for a firm to adopt the strictest rule everywhere than to run two product lines.
:::

# Three perspectives; delegated or entrepreneurial {background-color="#E3120B" style="color:#F7F4ED"}

## Brunsson, Rasche & Seidl (2012)

| Standardization… | Example |
|---|---|
| ***of*** organizations | ISO 14001 tells a firm how to organise environmental management |
| ***by*** organizations | the bodies that write standards, and how |
| ***as*** organization | standards ordering markets without hierarchy |

::: {.warn}
Standards are **dynamic**: revised, contested, translated — and **decoupled**. A certificate is not a practice.
:::

## Green (2013)

| | **Delegated** | **Entrepreneurial** |
|---|---|---|
| **Origin** | states hand over rule-making | private actors create rules others adopt |
| **Illustration** | verification under the Clean Development Mechanism | voluntary carbon accounting, e.g. the GHG Protocol |
| **Watch** | the state can take it back | adoption — the rule is as strong as its users |

# Race to the bottom, or trading up? {background-color="#E3120B" style="color:#F7F4ED"}

## Two scenarios

::::: columns

:::: {.column width="50%"}

### Race to the bottom

Trade intensifies competition → governments and firms cut environmental standards to win exports.

::::

:::: {.column width="50%"}

### Trading up — the California effect

Exporters to strict markets adopt strict standards → trade spreads them (Vogel, 1995).

::::

:::::

## Prakash & Potoski (2006)

- **ISO 14001**: voluntary, beyond what many domestic laws require
- **Panel**: 108 countries, seven years
- **Key variable**: adoption in a country's **export markets**

::: {.get}
**Finding:** trade linkages **encourage** ISO 14001 adoption when a country's major export markets have adopted it. Standards travel towards the customer's.
:::

::: {.muted}
*AJPS*, 50(2), 350–364. [doi:10.1111/j.1540-5907.2006.00188.x](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-5907.2006.00188.x)
:::

## For the firm

::: {.warn}
"Voluntary" is not "optional". A standard your buyers require is as binding as a law.
:::

- Monitor what your **customers' home markets** adopt, not only what your host government legislates
- Decide: **adopt** early, **shape** in the committee, or **resist** — each has a cost

> **Put it to the room:** two engineers, a quarter of their time, three years on an ISO committee. Worth it?

# The Tableau skill of the day {background-color="#E3120B" style="color:#F7F4ED"}

## Maps and Pages

1. `iso3` → *Geographic Role* → **Country/Region**
2. Check the **unknown** indicator → *Map → Edit Locations*
3. **Filled map** of certificates per billion US$ of GDP — sequential palette
4. `Year` → **Pages** shelf → press play
5. **Small multiples**: `Region` × `Year`, line of the median country

::: {.check}
Never join or geocode on names. Hong Kong, Taiwan, Korea and Türkiye will tell you why.
:::
